items.text:
PlayStation Plus Free Open-World RPG Is 6 Times Bigger Than Skyrim

Sony

Published Oct 17, 2026, 4:00 AM EDT

Ewan is Deputy Editor for ScreenRant's gaming section. He still quite hasn’t gotten out of his mid 00’s emo phase, and knows more about The Legend of Zelda and Doctor Who than is probably healthy.
Ewan oversees the content operation of ScreenRant's gaming output, working with a talented team of writers and editors to cover everything from the latest GTA 6 news to the indie games you need on your radar.
Former Editor of GAMINGbible, Ewan also has words at Kotaku, Den of Geek, NME, and UNILAD. He's appeared on various podcasts, including VGC's and BBC's Let's Talk About Tech.

If there are any PlayStation Plus gamers out there who want to spend the Christmas break getting good and lost in a massive open world game, I've got a suggestion for you. There are, of course, tons of great games to play on PlayStation Plus. So many it can be hard to know where to start, in fact. But if what you're after is a properly massive open world, how about one that's six times the size of Skyrim?

We all know size alone isn't the best measure of a great game: there are plenty of huge open-world games that are pretty awful. But there are games out there that do a really good job of balancing scope with a genuinely worthwhole sense of exploration.

This PlayStation Plus Game Is Truly Huge

It's also a genuine classic

It may be a familiar game, but it's always worth pointing out that the original Assassin's Creed Black Flag is completely free for PlayStation Plus Extra subscribers. And at a whopping 235 square kilometers, it outstrips Skyrim's own impressive map by roughly 37 square kilometers.

Now, it's worth pointing out that size isn't everything when it comes to video games. Just because an open world game is big doesn't automatically mean it's worth playing. It just so happens that Black Flag has a big open world and stands as one of the best Assassin's Creed games of all time.

I should stress that we're talking about the original game here and not this year's Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced. If you're gaming on a budget and fancy sailing around as a would-be assassin but don't want to pay for the remake, I can promise you the original version still holds up beautifully. Heck, I'd argue it's better in some aspects. I maintain the combat in the original is superior, for one thing, but that might just be me.

The world itself is actually worth exploring too, with a huge sea to sail across packed with secrets, islands, and lots of schmucks to assassinate. Whether you've played it before or not, the Christmas break could well be the perfect time to dive back into this all-time classic and remind yourself what Ubisoft can do when it's firing on all cylinders.

PlayStation Plus Has A Ton Of Assassin's Creed Games

You're spoiled for choice

If, for some mad reason, you've decided Assassin's Creed Black Flag isn't for you, then there are a bunch of other Assassin's Creed games available to play on PlayStation Plus.

There are currently 13 Assassin's Creed games on PlayStation Plus:

Assassin's Creed: The Ezio Collection

Assassin's Creed Unity

Assassin's Creed Syndicate

Assassin's Creed Chronicles: India

Assassin's Creed Chronicles: China

Assassin's Creed Chronicles: Russia

Assassin's Creed 3 Remastered

Assassin's Creed 4 Black Flag

Assassin's Creed Origins

Assassin's Creed Odyssey

Assassin's Creed Valhalla

Assassin's Creed Freedom Cry

Assassin's Creed Rogue remastered

A fat stack of games to be sure, and proof that PlayStation Plus subscribers aren't hurting for free games to play over the upcoming winter months.

items.title: New RPG From Final Fantasy, Persona Vets Borrows From The Past To Ask How We Can Save The Future
items.author: Alicia Haddick
items.summary: If, on one end of the spectrum, you have Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 and the Persona franchise returning turn-based RPGs to critical and commercial acclaim
items.text:
If, on one end of the spectrum, you have Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 and the Persona franchise returning turn-based RPGs to critical and commercial acclaim once again, and on the other you have modernized nostalgia packaged as HD-2D RPGs, then Eternal Anima sits somewhere in the middle. It’s a game that finds its own niche in the current, revitalized RPG field, even if it can at times feel a bit too much like a greatest hits compilation for the genre.

An all-new Japanese RPG developed by a team of industry veterans and notable outsiders at Marvelous, Eternal Anima is thematically driven by the responsibility that comes with inheriting the world and then passing it on to the next generation. How do the actions of our past ripple into the present and future, and how do those past choices shape the world that exists today?

Eternal Anima‘s director, Katsuhisa Higuchi, was a programmer on a number of early Final Fantasy games, also worked on Chrono Trigger and more recently served as a director on Capcom’s first two Monster Hunter Stories games. Kazushige Nojima is another Square Enix veteran, having worked on the story for Final Fantasy VII and VIII as well as the Kingdom Hearts series. The game’s narrative, meanwhile, is based on a concept submitted by acclaimed author Keisuke Makino, who has contributed to both Persona 5 and Metaphor: ReFantazio.

The story follows Wade, a man with the ability to see the history of objects merely by touching them. He lives in the world of Urvis Ael, where the truth about the past has been lost, and attempting to uncover it is forbidden. Hunted as a dissident, he journeys into the past, where he begins to discover the truth about how the world became the way it is. Perhaps by changing the past and exploring the continent of Ambulis which, in his time, has been submerged underwater and lost to history, he can fix his present and change the future (according to the game’s developers, you will later explore other continents facing similar strife, named Wistregen, Himeshiro and Rotala).

At an hour-long showcase of the game shortly before Tokyo Game Show last month, we were given a chance to check out a demo. It started off by placing us into an early adventure for Wade and his still-small crew of comrades not long after they arrive on Ambulis roughly 200 years in the past. The area they enter is called the Somber Woods, and it’s a place befitting such a name: far from a luscious forest, it’s an environment that’s dying around you. The planet’s Anima—essentially its life force—is being drained due to human exploitation of natural resources, with those sworn to protect it resigned to prayer and a belief that simply willing the land to solve the issue will suffice. No need to act or make changes to save the climate, it’ll be fine!

Our characters from the future, however, know what will happen. The continent will not be saved, and the world will die, all due to their inaction. They’re here to change its course.

So far, so typical for RPGs of the 1990s in which the fate of the world is at stake, but it’s how the game evolves beyond these tropes and integrates this thematic concern into all aspects, including gameplay, that makes Eternal Anima stand out. With our characters aware of how the future will play out if nothing is done, the game makes the ingenious choice to integrate this foresight into battle. The result transforms combat into something more like a puzzle, as instead of merely strategizing the best move, you seek to alter the predetermined trajectory of a fight.

The game employs a “break” system similar to that seen in games like Octopath Traveler, with the twist being that you know what move an opponent is going to make before they do it thanks to Wade’s Future Sight abilities. Above your command menu is a progress bar where you can see when and what move every opponent is going to use next. With this knowledge in mind and an awareness of their weaknesses, explicitly targeting them will delay their next attack. Halt an enemy’s actions long enough that you push them off the progress bar and you can “break” them, opening them up for massive damage.

Knowing how your opponent will act could have easily ruined the strategic aspect of combat. Instead, this knowledge only intensifies each battle into something more akin to a finely tuned puzzle than a typical RPG fight. I’d often spent exponentially longer on each turn than I typically do, pondering how to optimize my team’s attacks in order to break enemies and prevent my team from taking damage. All your tactical considerations are enhanced by the game’s BP system: each turn, allies earn an amount of BP that can both enhance an attack’s potency and increase the expected pushback on the turn progress bar when exploiting an enemy weakness. Perhaps it’s worth taking a small amount of damage in one turn to ensure that, when a boss’ most dangerous attack is ready to strike, you have the BP to ensure a vital break that can prevent a team wipeout.

“Through Future Sight you can see when enemies will attack, what attacks they will use, who will take damage and how much,” explains Makoto Shioda, the game’s producer. “Players peer into the future before choosing their actions, so their actions can change that predicted future. For example, if you see that an enemy’s upcoming powerful attack will kill one of your party members, you can defeat that enemy first to make sure your party member never takes damage and therefore survive.”

In simple fights against random enemies in the field, it’s hardly necessary to think too deeply about these intricacies. Against bosses, however? It’s essential. Simply finding one weakness won’t win a battle, either, as the game prevents repeated exploitation of the same vulnerability to enforce variety in combat. The result is a system that’s easy to get accustomed to, but also appears fiendishly deep and difficult to master.

And that’s about all I can say about what to expect from the game. While we got glimpses of the broader overarching story, we were stripped of key context about how the past and present interact in the story, the identity of the game’s major antagonists, and the circumstances that led them onto their quest.

What we did get to see sometimes felt more like an homage to the legendary games the developers worked on in the past than an expression of the game’s unique identity. M.O.S., the robot sidekick of the team, feels almost like a carbon copy of Robo in Chrono Trigger. The village of La Boset near the Somber Woods is similarly derivative, though the concept of elders who don’t know what is best for their home, still believing that living alongside nature is the same as listening to and caring for it, is at least a pretty interesting approach to this trope. Issues with “parallels to the real world we live in” promise to be central to the game, according to Katsuhisa Higuchi, the game’s director.

Even if the game describes itself as a love letter to RPGs of the past, I’m curious to see how it can define itself beyond those historic references and establish itself as something more, especially with legacy serving as such a central idea to the game. As Higuchi concluded to us, “While we did not consider our real-world legacy when deciding to make it the game’s theme, I can say that we did consider it as development progressed and factored in our feelings towards Japanese RPGs. I did develop a strong sense that where we are now is a culmination of all that has been passed down prior to today.”

Hunted as a dissident, he journeys into the past, where he begins to discover the truth about how the world became the way it is. Perhaps by changing the past and exploring the continent of Ambulis which, in his time, has been submerged underwater and lost to history, he can fix his present and change the future (according to the game’s developers, you will later explore other continents facing similar strife, named Wistregen, Himeshiro and Rotala).
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/10/system-shock-2.jpg
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/10/EN14-02-1.jpg
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/10/Eternal-Anima-06.jpg

At an hour-long showcase of the game shortly before Tokyo Game Show last month, we were given a chance to check out a demo. It started off by placing us into an early adventure for Wade and his still-small crew of comrades not long after they arrive on Ambulis roughly 200 years in the past. The area they enter is called the Somber Woods, and it’s a place befitting such a name: far from a luscious forest, it’s an environment that’s dying around you. The planet’s Anima—essentially its life force—is being drained due to human exploitation of natural resources, with those sworn to protect it resigned to prayer and a belief that simply willing the land to solve the issue will suffice. No need to act or make changes to save the climate, it’ll be fine!
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/10/ff7-rev.jpg
Our characters from the future, however, know what will happen. The continent will not be saved, and the world will die, all due to their inaction. They’re here to change its course.
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/10/anatolia.jpg

So far, so typical for RPGs of the 1990s in which the fate of the world is at stake, but it’s how the game evolves beyond these tropes and integrates this thematic concern into all aspects, including gameplay, that makes Eternal Anima stand out. With our characters aware of how the future will play out if nothing is done, the game makes the ingenious choice to integrate this foresight into battle. The result transforms combat into something more like a puzzle, as instead of merely strategizing the best move, you seek to alter the predetermined trajectory of a fight.
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/10/Grand-Theft-Auto-6-Launch-Trailer-image-Rockstar-Games-160x160.jpg
blocks.c: Grand Theft Auto 6 Launch Trailer Image Rockstar Games

blocks.x: The game employs a “break” system similar to that seen in games like Octopath Traveler, with the twist being that you know what move an opponent is going to make before they do it thanks to Wade’s Future Sight abilities. Above your command menu is a progress bar where you can see when and what move every opponent is going to use next. With this knowledge in mind and an awareness of their weaknesses, explicitly targeting them will delay their next attack. Halt an enemy’s actions long enough that you push them off the progress bar and you can “break” them, opening them up for massive damage.
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/10/khsora-160x160.jpg
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/10/Eternal-Anima-03.jpg

Knowing how your opponent will act could have easily ruined the strategic aspect of combat. Instead, this knowledge only intensifies each battle into something more akin to a finely tuned puzzle than a typical RPG fight. I’d often spent exponentially longer on each turn than I typically do, pondering how to optimize my team’s attacks in order to break enemies and prevent my team from taking damage. All your tactical considerations are enhanced by the game’s BP system: each turn, allies earn an amount of BP that can both enhance an attack’s potency and increase the expected pushback on the turn progress bar when exploiting an enemy weakness. Perhaps it’s worth taking a small amount of damage in one turn to ensure that, when a boss’ most dangerous attack is ready to strike, you have the BP to ensure a vital break that can prevent a team wipeout.
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/10/elizabeth-holmes-160x160.jpg

“Through Future Sight you can see when enemies will attack, what attacks they will use, who will take damage and how much,” explains Makoto Shioda, the game’s producer. “Players peer into the future before choosing their actions, so their actions can change that predicted future. For example, if you see that an enemy’s upcoming powerful attack will kill one of your party members, you can defeat that enemy first to make sure your party member never takes damage and therefore survive.”
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/10/cammy-160x160.jpg
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/10/GettyImages-2295116957-1-160x160.jpg

In simple fights against random enemies in the field, it’s hardly necessary to think too deeply about these intricacies. Against bosses, however? It’s essential. Simply finding one weakness won’t win a battle, either, as the game prevents repeated exploitation of the same vulnerability to enforce variety in combat. The result is a system that’s easy to get accustomed to, but also appears fiendishly deep and difficult to master.
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/07/Belmont-160x160.jpg
blocks.c: Art shows a woman fighting a Harpy.

blocks.x: And that’s about all I can say about what to expect from the game. While we got glimpses of the broader overarching story, we were stripped of key context about how the past and present interact in the story, the identity of the game’s major antagonists, and the circumstances that led them onto their quest.
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/07/image-15-160x160.jpg
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/10/Eternal-Anima-02.jpg

What we did get to see sometimes felt more like an homage to the legendary games the developers worked on in the past than an expression of the game’s unique identity. M.O.S., the robot sidekick of the team, feels almost like a carbon copy of Robo in Chrono Trigger. The village of La Boset near the Somber Woods is similarly derivative, though the concept of elders who don’t know what is best for their home, still believing that living alongside nature is the same as listening to and caring for it, is at least a pretty interesting approach to this trope. Issues with “parallels to the real world we live in” promise to be central to the game, according to Katsuhisa Higuchi, the game’s director.
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/10/something-fun-160x160.jpg

Even if the game describes itself as a love letter to RPGs of the past, I’m curious to see how it can define itself beyond those historic references and establish itself as something more, especially with legacy serving as such a central idea to the game. As Higuchi concluded to us, “While we did not consider our real-world legacy when deciding to make it the game’s theme, I can say that we did consider it as development progressed and factored in our feelings towards Japanese RPGs. I did develop a strong sense that where we are now is a culmination of all that has been passed down prior to today.”

items.title: “Tulsa King,” and Stallone, Start to Show Their Age in Season 4
items.author: Clint Worthington
items.summary: Of the universe of Taylor Sheridan AARP-for-aging-’80s-guys dramas aimed squarely at the silent majority, “Tulsa King” is by far the most charming. Flitting
items.text:
Of the universe of Taylor Sheridan AARP-for-aging-’80s-guys dramas aimed squarely at the silent majority, “Tulsa King” is by far the most charming. Flitting somewhere between “Yellowstone” and “Get Shorty” in its tale of a New York goombah (Sylvester Stallone) starting his criminal enterprise all over again in Oklahoma, the show has spent three seasons simply letting its bulging cast of characters engage in soap-opera theatrics, squaring off against rival gang members and, in this last set of episodes, a vindictive bourbon distiller played by Robert Patrick. (Spoiler alert: Sly burns him at the stake in the season finale. I guess it’s the only way to be sure with the T-1000.) But in season four, “Tulsa King” finally feels like it’s getting lost in the literal and metaphorical sauce.

After taking over Patrick’s distillery, Dwight “The General” Manfredi (Stallone) is finally ready to legitimize his enterprises (well, some of them) and settle down with his girlfriend of three seasons, Margaret Devereaux (Dana Delany). Unfortunately, mysterious circumstances arise at the end of the season premiere that leave Dwight in deep mourning and unsure where his businesses stand with the government. That latter concern is compounded by the elevation of lieutenant governor Amanda Clark (Gretchen Mol), a by-the-books do-gooder who knows Dwight’s game and wants to shut him down permanently, to the top office.

That’s not Dwight’s only concern, of course; his old mafia family in New York City keeps gunning for the profits he’s been building in the Southwest, especially now that his old nemesis, Quiet Ray (James Russo), is fully in charge. What’s more, a greedy German AI tech bro (Flula Borg) is threatening to take Margaret’s horse ranch by eminent domain to turn the land into a data center.

(L-R): Scarlet Stallone as Spencer, Martin Starr as Bodhi, and Jay Will as Tyson in Tulsa King, episode 1, season 4, streaming on Paramount+, 2026. Photo Credit: Steve Swisher/Paramount+

All these conflicts and more stud “Tulsa King”‘s new season, and that’s not even getting into Bodhi’s (Martin Starr) flirtation with wine forgery, or Tyson’s (Jay Will) burgeoning rap career. And let’s not forget Dwight’s unsteady alliance with government spook Musso (Kevin Pollak) from last season and how that dovetails with Dwight’s existing animus with fellow capo Bevilaqua (Frank Grillo). Hey, there are a lot of aging character actors to pay; we gotta give them something to do, right? We should be thankful Samuel L. Jackson isn’t here to soak up more screen time, as he’s supposedly off building his own spinoff down in New Orleans.

“Tulsa King,” at this point, is more overstuffed than a turducken, with a cast so bloated that the gang is juggling at least three or four different schemes at once. Even Sly is getting a little tired; sure, some of that is Dwight’s puffed-up grief, but some of it is the older actor slowing down. (The show even writes a cane into Dwight’s ensemble; it’s passed off as an occasional knee injury that flares up from time to time, but I get the feeling that cane’s here to stay.) Even Sly coasting is compelling enough to watch, but you can tell the rest of the cast has to shore up their game to help carry this thing. This is especially true of Annabella Sciorra’s Joanne, Dwight’s enterprising sister and partner in crime, who slowly becomes the show’s heart and soul.

Gretchen Mol as Amanda Clark in Tulsa King, season 4, streaming on Paramount+, 2026. Photo Credit: Steve Swisher/Paramount+

In fact, you get the most enjoyment from showrunner Dave Erickson and his writing team’s occasional lapses into the ridiculous. Italian enforcer pals Goodie (Chris Caldovino) and Vince (Vincent Piazza) shoot their way out of a white supremacist meeting at a restaurant they happen to be eating at; “You just got robbed by two swarthy Mediterraneans!” they shout as they leave. Dwight mournfully asks an AI chatbot whether God exists, and the scene is treated as if it’s dispensing therapeutic wisdom from on high. Someone gets their head crushed in the jaws of a fossilized dinosaur skull. In these scenes, “Tulsa King” ekes out a kind of campy enjoyment. It’s just a shame you have to sift through so many diluted storylines to get there. (The less said about the budding romance between Garrett Hedlund’s Mitch and Scarlet Stallone’s Spencer, the better.)

It’d be dishonest to claim “Tulsa King” doesn’t offer consistent diversion, even amid the myriad components of Dwight’s business empire and all the spinning plates therein. But this season’s villains don’t compel (including everyone’s favorite “My Son Hunter” director Robert Davi as a creaky enforcer who looks like he can barely stand, let alone take out fools), and so many of the plot threads feel like filler to give Dwight’s bloated entourage things to do. The bulk of the show’s charm falls squarely on Stallone’s broad shoulders, and even he’s starting to lose a step. Here’s hoping the show can get its affairs in order in an already-announced season five, or this vital leg of the Taylor Sheridan universe will go, well, the way of the dinosaur.

Full season screened for review. Premieres October 16th on Paramount+.

items.title: PlayStation 6 Price Tag Has Gamers Ready To Ditch Consoles Forever
items.author: Ewan Moore
items.summary:
PlayStation 6 Price Tag Has Gamers Ready To Ditch Consoles Forever

Published Oct 17, 2026, 3:21 AM EDT

Ewan is Deputy Editor for ScreenRant's gaming section.
items.text:
PlayStation 6 Price Tag Has Gamers Ready To Ditch Consoles Forever

Published Oct 17, 2026, 3:21 AM EDT

Ewan is Deputy Editor for ScreenRant's gaming section. He still quite hasn’t gotten out of his mid 00’s emo phase, and knows more about The Legend of Zelda and Doctor Who than is probably healthy.
Ewan oversees the content operation of ScreenRant's gaming output, working with a talented team of writers and editors to cover everything from the latest GTA 6 news to the indie games you need on your radar.
Former Editor of GAMINGbible, Ewan also has words at Kotaku, Den of Geek, NME, and UNILAD. He's appeared on various podcasts, including VGC's and BBC's Let's Talk About Tech.

With PlayStation and other console makers continuing to raise the price of the current generation of consoles, gamers everywhere are looking to the next generation with genuine concern that they might finally be priced out of a hobby they love.

Sony's latest console, the PlayStation 5 Pro now costs $899.99 as of the most recent price hike. By comparison, the base PlayStation 5 is $599.99, which means it's now an extra $200 more than it was at launch. This is unheard of, for a console celebrating its six-year anniversary to be more expensive than it was at launch, but with the increasing costs of hardware and tariffs, it's hardly surprising.

The PlayStation 6 Could Cost Up To $1,000

With rumors swirling that the PlayStation 6 might not be so far away, what does this mean for gamers? According to consultant Dr. Serkan Toto, the PlayStation 6, which is rumored to launch as early as 2027, could cost upwards of $1000, making it the first console to hit that four-figure sum.

In an interview with Games Radar, industry researcher Joost van Dreunen agreed with Toto, saying, “We're quickly moving towards a world in which a $1,000 console will be the norm, and console gaming will become a luxury expenditure."

“They really don't want to raise prices on their hardware, because that part is usually a heavily subsidized part of the equation and the sale of games is the gravity point of their revenue model. I predict that the next generation of console hardware will start at a 50% higher price point than the current one did.”

This is also a sentiment shared by Circana analyst Mat Piscatella, who added, “Could we see $1,000 pricing? Sure, that's possible. I would really hate to see that, but it's possible.”

In an investor Q&A from June this year, Sony touched on pricing for future hardware. As reported by VGC, the company stated: "As a principle, we do not intend to sell hardware at significant losses. At the same time, we are carefully monitoring the market and continuing to evaluate our approach. We believe it is important for us to make every effort to ensure that customers fully understand the value we provide in relation to pricing."

There Aren't Too Many Gamers Who Want To Pay So Much

Sony has been one of the big players since the PlayStation released in 1994, and it's cultivated a hardcore fanbase over the last 30 years. But as the cost of pretty much everything continues to rise, the concept of a $1000 console becomes an even tougher pill to swallow than it would have been even a few years ago.

"If the next generation comes at a $1000 price point I will ride my Series X as long as it lasts and then maybe consider buying a used next gen console," writes one Reddit gamer. "If they can be had for a reasonable price."

Another added: "$1000 consoles to play $100 mediocre games that take 6 years to make and you won't even own. Yeah, they can keep their 'new' generation."

"I can't think of a future where consoles aren't dead if this goes on," said a third. "Why drop $1000 on a digital only console that has one storefront controlled by the people that made the console when you could build a decent PC for $1500-$2000 it'll last longer, it'll play more games, and you have multiple storefronts to choose from."

With many agreeing that committing to a gaming PC will be more worth it in the long run, whilst others hoping that their PlayStation 5 will still keep them going for the next few years, it seems as though Sony is going to see some much lower figures when it comes to the unit sales of the PlayStation 6.

items.title: Star Wars Genesis Is The Open-World Star Wars RPG I Always Wanted
items.author: Ewan Moore
items.summary: It's a heck of a time to be a Star Wars fan, isn't it? Over in the world of video games, we've got both Star Wars: Fate Of The Old Republic and Star Wars Jedi
items.text:
It's a heck of a time to be a Star Wars fan, isn't it? Over in the world of video games, we've got both Star Wars: Fate Of The Old Republic and Star Wars Jedi 3 on the horizon. But with both games yet to receive an actual release date, what's a Star Wars fan to do while they wait? I've got some ideas.

If you're looking to scratch the Star Wars RPG itch, Star Wars Genesis keeps getting bigger and better all the time, cementing itself as one of the greatest Star Wars roleplaying experiences of all-time. The latest update, 8.83, is a feature-packed update that completely changes the game once again, and is well worth your time.

What Is Star Wars Genesis?

You've probably seen it around

Star Wars Genesis has been around for a little while, but it really went viral over Christmas. For those who don't know, it's actually a total conversion modlist for Starfield, but one so massively detailed that you might never know it used to be another game. The project's developer DeityVengy has just released version 8.6, and it is packed with new stuff. The game is working towards a big 10.0 update with new quests, characters, and the essential aim of providing a complete and total conversion. That's not to say the latest build isn't worth your time.

You can take a look below for the full rundown, but highlights of Genesis right now include a brand-new questline, new music, improved loading times, a companion system, and even more converted cities. Oh, and while it's not mentioned in the list below, lightsabers are available in the game. Just in case you were holding off so you could play as a Jedi.

Star Wars: Genesis – Features

Unique Main Story Questline

Complete Sound and Music Overhaul

Full Conversion of ALL Factions

5 Additional Star Wars Factions

Full Conversion of ALL Weapons+

Full Conversion of ALL Armors+

Full Conversion of ALL Droids+

Expansive Prop Conversions

Notable Locations and Planets

30,000+ Converted Voicelines

Alien Races (NPCs and Player)

Droids (NPCs and Player)

Custom Standalone Cities and Planets

Unique Armor Progression Loop

Converted Cities

Force Powers

Aurebesh Environment Overhaul

Iconic Ships and Vehicles

Unique Side Quests and Lore

Lore Accurate Armor Hierarchy

Unique Main Cast

Named Crew Overhaul

300+ Repeatable Sandbox Missions

Custom Holographic HUD

Gameplay & Systems Improvements

Automated Install

Reduced Loading Screens

Vanilla Bug Fixes

Immersive Alternate Start

Third Person Animation Revamp

Realistic Damage and Scaling

Improved Ragdolls

Smarter AI

Triple Armor Variety

Double Weapon Variety

Rebalanced Economy

POI and Worldgen Overhaul

Unique Sub-Factions

Complete Biome Overhaul

Dynamic Weather Overhaul

Enhanced Character Creation

Optional 4K Textures & Visuals

Vanilla Gameplay Improvements

NPC Schedules and Cycles

City Light Day/Night Cycle

Custom Bosses and Dungeons

Rare Encounters

Skill Revamp

Doubled Music Variety

Star Wars Fans Can't Miss This

Just remember it's PC only

As much as I'd love to be able to play this myself, I should point out that Star Wars Genesis isn't available on the Xbox Series X|S version of Starfield. While there are a few Star Wars mods that can be downloaded on Xbox via the console's mod support, Genesis is just way too complicated, and getting more complicated with each passing update. As such, you'll only ever be able to play it on PC.

If you do have a PC that can handle it, and you are a Star Wars fan, what are you waiting for? This could be the most fun you ever have with Starfield.

TV Show(s)

The Mandalorian, Andor, Obi-Wan Kenobi, The Book of Boba Fett, Ahsoka, The Acolyte, Star Wars: Skeleton Crew, Lando, Star Wars: The Clone Wars, Star Wars Rebels, Star Wars: The Bad Batch, Star Wars: Resistance, Star Wars: Young Jedi Adventures, Star Wars: Visions

Video Game(s)

items.text:
“Bring Order To Chaos.” That’s how tactical shooter Ready or Not sums up your role as part of Special Weapons and Tactics, or SWAT. As a commander, you lead an “element” of four officers through a gauntlet of ripped-from-the-headlines catastrophes in fictional Los Suenõs, California—the “City of Dreams,” not angels. Some missions merely touch a nerve, while others evoke mononymic American tragedies like Columbine, Pulse, Waco, or Vegas with the serial numbers filed off. Developer VOID Interactive has stated that it intends Ready or Not to immerse players in split-second, volatile situations, leaving them with an appreciation for the totalizing physical and psychological strain these officers endure for our sake.

Order comes to chaos at the end of a gun. You mash X to scream “I wanna see hands!” at everyone in sight, civilians and gunmen alike. It’ll piss you off when they don’t comply. You’re here to help. Non-lethal means of submission will net you the best rating at the end of a mission, but nobody’s perfect.

Indulge me in a quick history break. In Rise of the Warrior Cop, Radley Balko says the 1965 Watts riots were “the first major incident to push America toward more militarized policing.” Infamous LAPD chief Daryl Gates is credited with creating SWAT proper after his experience during the riots, which the LAPD had “no idea” how to handle. Nearly 30 years later, Daryl Gates would produce Sierra’s 1993 Police Quest: Open Season, the fourth entry in the series.

Gates was fresh out of the LAPD in ’93, having taken the fall for an entire culture of brutal, racist policing, including but by no means limited to the 1991 beating of Rodney King and the riots sparked a year later by the acquittal of King’s attackers. By the ’90s, Balko says most teams weren’t responding to “urban warfare” situations of the sort the division was created to handle: they were breaking down doors on drug raids. A militarized police needs a war to fight.

Police Quest was rebranded as SWAT in 1999, and Ready or Not is widely referred to as the spiritual successor to Irrational Games’ SWAT 4—VOID Interactive even hired SWAT 4 modders in the early days of development.

BACK-OF-THE-BOX QUOTE

"Get on the ground. NOW!!!"

TYPE OF GAME

Squad-based first-person shooter with multiplayer

LIKED

Evil heart of America. Methodical pace. Meticulous level design. High-pressure shooting.

DISLIKED

Evil heart of America. Weapon fetish. The post office level.

Developer

Void Interactive

Platform

PS5 (played), Xbox Series X/S, PC

Release Date

December 13, 2023

Played

20 hours. Single-player, some score-chasing.

VOID Interactive is aware it’s working with hot-button material. The game is careful to toe an apparently neutral line of tastefulness by gesturing/dog-whistling to left and right ideologies alike. The enemies in one mission are a Vietnamese family modifying semi-automatic weapons into fully automatic ones in order to pay for their mother’s cancer treatment, which is pure liberal pathos. Contrast that with a mission where you clear an abandoned building full of homeless people taking shelter from a hurricane, most of whom open fire on sight or mindlessly rush you like Condemned: Criminal Origins mooks—a peek into the nightmares of people who ask you if Chicago is really that violent.

The game’s plot is loose and non-linear, but if you poke through pre-mission briefings and evidence, it’s clear that everything from fake-ISIS to MKUltra, Hollywood sickos to 4chan trolls are besieging Los Suenõs. Drug cartels? Sure. Russians? Got ’em. Armed…misandrist…cults? Okay! The specifics, nonsensical as they are, suggest an overarching, Mark Wahlberg-ian fantasy of intervention in historical mass shootings. You’re here to right wrongs. The rest is flavor. Paramilitaries in a Vegas hotel or a group of kids holding up a gas station: any one of them could draw a weapon or take a civilian hostage. Get on the fucking ground!

Academic and Twitter user Ian Bogost coined the term “persuasive games,” saying they “strive to alter or affect player opinion outside of the game, not merely to cause him [sic] to continue playing.” While the politics, the milieu, and the mechanics of Ready Or Not are far removed from essentially any game anyone has ever described this way, it’s absolutely in this lineage. It really wants you to understand how it feels to be first on the scene with an active shooter in the vicinity. It wants you to feel the psychological weight of these decisions—decisions that are awful and unenviable but completely necessary to maintain the modern American standard of living. These are good men who do the ugly work of rooting out evil. So go vote “yes” on next year’s police budget.

The idea of games as empathy machines was in vogue about a decade ago: think Depression Quest; Cart Life; That Dragon, Cancer; Problem Attic, or Papers, Please. Ready or Not is more viscerally effective at communicating its worldview than just about any “empathy game” or autofictional itch.io curio I’ve ever played. It happens to be a worldview I find totally abhorrent. Of course the Tijuana border tunnel mission is ugly to sit through in the midst of ICE’s heightened campaign of terror. Call of Duty‘s addled geopolitics don’t hit with this kind of clarity. It’s useless to moralize: the sick thrill is the point.

Playing Ready or Not is like being force-fed pure fearmongering. It’s a wonder there isn’t a mission set in a Planned Parenthood. You scream at the civilians to get on the ground and the game screams at you. This is how it is. This is the world we live in. This is what must be done.

items.author: Kenneth Shepard
items.summary: From the moment Legendary Pictures and Capcom revealed its new live-action Street Fighter, there was a ceiling placed above it. This movie could either be so
items.text:
From the moment Legendary Pictures and Capcom revealed its new live-action Street Fighter, there was a ceiling placed above it. This movie could either be so bad it’s good or so bad it’s just bad. There wasn’t a third option, at least, that’s what I thought for around a year. It turns out, there is a third option: it’s both.

Street Fighter is basically two movies in one: It is one half the aforementioned “so bad it’s good” flick, running into walls hard enough to break through them as it shatters the shackles of a faithful adaptation and becomes an incomprehensible parody of Capcom’s fighting games. Also equally present is the “so bad it’s bad” film that is baffling from both a filmmaking and storytelling perspective. Both of these movies are connected by fights that are fun to watch and disconnected by ones it refuses to show. The strained threads that manage to hold it all together are a constant barrage of bits of varying quality that every actor commits to with such tenacity that it all somehow turns around to being brilliant?

To be clear: Street Fighter’s a bad movie. It’s incoherent, edited in ways that don’t make any sense, and the gap between its best performances and worst ones is wider than the skill difference between a mediocre player picking up Street Fighter for the first time and the all-time great Daigo Umehara. Also, the way it treats the few women on the roster, performing character assassination on Cammy by essentially turning her from a stoic, duty-driven Doll into a crazed Juri stand-in and injecting some truly out-of-pocket horniness into Chun-Li’s scenes at the expense of their gravity, sucks ass. But after watching Street Fighter, my friends and I sat together for hours untangling this messy hairball of a movie, and the more we did so, the more we started to see the vision. Half the vision is just kind of garbage.

Though the massive ensemble cast brings so many of the biggest names in Street FIghter back to the big screen, the movie is primarily a Ken and Ryu story, cranking up their history as friendly rivals into one of deep-rooted jealousy and resentment. After years apart, the two are reunited at the World Warrior tournament, which is just a front for the psycho-powered tyrant M. Bison’s plans to siphon Ryu’s growing powers into himself. Amidst all this, Chun-Li is undercover as a double agent working for Bison but operating with her own agenda, and a whole lot of other Street Fighter mainstays show up in-between the serious shit, and while they’re mostly relegated to bit players, by golly, they are effective. Cody Rhodes as Guile is a certified scene stealer and Jason Momoa’s Blanka is an actual good example of what happens when an actor has truly stopped giving a shit (complimentary), in stark contrast to his role in Minecraft.

The cast’s ability to deliver rapid-fire nonsense with a straight face is what elevates Street Fighter beyond straight camp and into a sometimes-hilarious martial arts comedy, in between the many, many jokes that don’t land. For every good gag, you get something tired and extremely dated that feels straight out of a movie from its ‘90s setting that lands with a groan-inducing thud. Then it somehow balances the gay jokes out by being extremely homoerotic any chance it gets. Again, Street Fighter is multiple movies in one, coalescing into a trainwreck that erupts in a magnificent explosion of fire and chaotic destruction. Almost nothing it does is in service to anything beyond the bit. The movie cannot resist submerging everything in a thick, self-aware irony, whether it’s the writing or its music choices straight out of a Gen X or elder Millennial’s nostalgia playlist.

This steadfast unwillingness to take anything seriously extends to even the most serious characters in the series becoming spoofs of themselves. M. Bison? The despot trying to suck the superpowered life force out of Ryu? Street Fighter makes a whole thing out of him probably having a foot fetish, and there is more than one shot of actor David Dastmalchian’s eyes rolling back into his head like he’s mid-climax. Also, there are a surprising amount of dudes cumming in this movie. It happens more than once.

A movie this dumb and batshit feels like something that should be immune to meaningful dissection because almost none of it is meaningful. It is the movie equivalent of a group of sleep-deprived fighting game players riffing on their collective vocal stims in a voice chat. But even under those pretenses, Street Fighter is just an oddly constructed film. It’s so bloated in its two-hour runtime that it is constantly flashing back and forth between multiple plot threads in one scene, regardless of if they’re connected at all. The editing of some segments, such as one in which the movie obscures the middle section of a conversation between Ken and Chun-Li only to splice what we missed into the very next segment for no real benefit, confounds me. And, perhaps most notably, the larger cast is exceptionally underutilized. When the actual tournament began and it was revealed that Guile and Vega had it out off-screen, I realized that we were going to miss out on a lot of actual street fighting in the Street Fighter movie.

The fights we do get are choreographed well and even I am not immune to the key-jingling of watching the actors pull off their characters’ signature moves, but some characters like Zangief and Guile only get to have it out in a group bar fight rather than in the ring. There are a lot of fighters in this movie, but we only see a handful of them really partake in the scrap. As a Ryu main, I got to see my boy toss a few fireballs, but if you’re hoping every character gets some big fight where they get to cycle through all your favorite moves, you’re gonna be disappointed.

A lesser movie would have nothing but a mess to show for all this spectacle, but Street Fighter’s tireless devotion to the bit somehow manages to salvage everything that makes it terrible into an incredible group watch. It’s hard to communicate the way this movie straddles the line between good and bad without sounding like you’re just describing how every other bad fighting game adaptation does it. But unlike something like the Dead or Alive movie or the modern Mortal Kombat, the group watch isn’t so you can all make fun of Street Fighter; it’s so you can all sit around after and realize that the movie has just as much sauce as it does horseshit.

Street Fighter makes a whole thing out of him probably having a foot fetish, and there is more than one shot of actor David Dastmalchian’s eyes rolling back into his head like he’s mid-climax. Also, there are a surprising amount of dudes cumming in this movie. It happens more than once.

A movie this dumb and batshit feels like something that should be immune to meaningful dissection because almost none of it is meaningful. It is the movie equivalent of a group of sleep-deprived fighting game players riffing on their collective vocal stims in a voice chat. But even under those pretenses, Street Fighter is just an oddly constructed film. It’s so bloated in its two-hour runtime that it is constantly flashing back and forth between multiple plot threads in one scene, regardless of if they’re connected at all. The editing of some segments, such as one in which the movie obscures the middle section of a conversation between Ken and Chun-Li only to splice what we missed into the very next segment for no real benefit, confounds me. And, perhaps most notably, the larger cast is exceptionally underutilized. When the actual tournament began and it was revealed that Guile and Vega had it out off-screen, I realized that we were going to miss out on a lot of actual street fighting in the Street Fighter movie.

The fights we do get are choreographed well and even I am not immune to the key-jingling of watching the actors pull off their characters’ signature moves, but some characters like Zangief and Guile only get to have it out in a group bar fight rather than in the ring. There are a lot of fighters in this movie, but we only see a handful of them really partake in the scrap. As a Ryu main, I got to see my boy toss a few fireballs, but if you’re hoping every character gets some big fight where they get to cycle through all your favorite moves, you’re gonna be disappointed.
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/07/image-15-160x160.jpg

A lesser movie would have nothing but a mess to show for all this spectacle, but Street Fighter’s tireless devotion to the bit somehow manages to salvage everything that makes it terrible into an incredible group watch. It’s hard to communicate the way this movie straddles the line between good and bad without sounding like you’re just describing how every other bad fighting game adaptation does it. But unlike something like the Dead or Alive movie or the modern Mortal Kombat, the group watch isn’t so you can all make fun of Street Fighter; it’s so you can all sit around after and realize that the movie has just as much sauce as it does horseshit.

items.title: 2026 Has Already Seen More Games Added To Steam Than All Of 2025, And It’s About To Get So Much Worse
items.author: John Walker
items.summary: According to SteamDB, a total of 21,248 new games were added to Valve’s PC store in 2025. That was almost 3,000 more than 2024, which itself beat 2023 by over
items.text:
According to SteamDB, a total of 21,248 new games were added to Valve’s PC store in 2025. That was almost 3,000 more than 2024, which itself beat 2023 by over 4,000. 2026 is going to smash that record again, and we know this because it already has, and it’s only mid-October. But this could be nothing compared to what we’ll see in 2027.

As spotted by Bredan Keogh on BlueSky, today marks the moment that Steam releases during 2026 exceeded those from all of 2025. We’re now at a total of 21,388, with two-and-a-half months of the year—traditionally the busiest ones for game releases—still remaining. SteamPageAnalyzer is projecting that the total will reach at least 24,000.

This is, obviously, a silly number of games. It breaks down to 66 games releasing each day, up from 55 in 2025, creating a market that’s ever more cluttered and in which a growing number of extremely good games will drown. This sucks, but thankfully is something Steam owner Valve is slowly working on, with recent ideas like the prominent front-page spot for Your Personal Calendar. This is a ten-box section of games the Steam algo suspects you’ll be interested in playing, whether because you’ve previously wishlisted them, or because they match the sorts of games you tend to play, and it’s pretty good at doing it. Some developers are also anecdotally reporting that it’s helping their games get seen by the people more likely to buy them, and hopefully Valve will lean in and continue to innovate in these areas. Except, this could be about to get a whole lot harder.

Vibe-coded game, are springing up increasingly frequently, and with recent changes to Claude allowing the quick and easy decompilation of other developers’ games, it’s already starting to get much worse.

Back in July, Nicole Carpenter reported on the growing power of vibe coding, explaining how it made creating rip-offs of existing games something that takes only a matter of hours. And this month it became far, far more common thanks to Anthropic’s latest Claude Opus 5.5, leading to web-based versions of established games springing up faster than they can be taken down, and worse, being extremely good at the process.

Given Steam has long been home to avalanches of the latest form of low-grade gaming crap, whether it’s achievement-farming idle games, “desktop companion games,” or whatever the slop du jour might be, it’s now victim to the inescapable lava flow of vibe-coded guff. So just imagine where things will be in 2027.

The one limitation to getting a game on Steam, beyond the spurious verification processes, is a $100 charge. This nominal fee, intended to try to put off chancers who intend to release a barely-functioning asset flip from bothering, is clearly failing in its role, and with vibe-coded knock-offs likely to become the norm, such games will only become actually better to play, and thus more likely to make some money.

Unless Valve takes some serious steps to curb the onslaught of AI-created games on its store (and right now you cannot even filter new release lists to remove games with AI declarations), I find it hard to believe we’ll see fewer than 30,000 games released on Steam in 2027, possibly far more. No matter how much algorithm-driven curation there might be, it’ll only get harder for an unknown but great game to find its way to the surface amidst such carnage.

items.title: CD Projekt is in "a really dangerous place", says Anthem's executive producer, pointing to ballooning costs of making games of that scope and quality
items.author: Julian Benson
items.summary: "The triple-A industry has become over-specialised, specialised to the point of hyper-fragility," Mark Darrah states in a foreboding interview found deep in
items.text:
"The triple-A industry has become over-specialised, specialised to the point of hyper-fragility," Mark Darrah states in a foreboding interview found deep in the pages of the Summer Eternal Anthology, recently covered by Edwin. As a former executive producer at Bioware, who corralled teams on Anthem and Dragon Age, after starting his career as a programmer on Baldur's Gate, Neverwinter Nights, and Jade Empire, Darrah has seen firsthand the growing scale of video game production and the challenges it can bring.

Darrah's also been vocal about the difficult development of Anthem in the past, and the struggles he had at Bioware. However, while what he says in the interview may be familiar, I found it gained sharper definition when read in light of games industry news and some of the interviews I've had with developers this year. So let me pull together some of the choice bits with the extra context from our own RPS vaults.

I should say, I've not laid hands myself on the Summer Eternal Anthology - a 500-page manifesto/design document/making-of book for Red Rooster, the new RPG from a splinter group of former Disco Elysium developers. But Edwin, who acknowledges that he's acknowledged in the acknowledgements section, did send me some photos of the interview with Darrah that's found deep within its pages.

Anyway, back to the Darrah's warning of over-specialisation. One of the problems, he says, is that it's caused teams to balloon in size because "No one person can add anything into a triple-A game. It requires at least five people." Obviously, the immediate implication of this is that larger teams cost more to run. The more staff you have on payroll, the more you will need to pay out each month on salaries, the more office space you will need to rent, the more software licenses and equipment you will need to pay for. This isn't the first time this has been said, just last month I ran an interview with Saber Interactive's chief creative officer Tim Willits, who put some numbers on those costs. "Each one of those developers is expensive," Willits said. "You have 200 people that you're paying $15,000 per person per month, which gets you way over two million."

But Darrah then links the complexity of projects to the increased risk of a delay. "The reality is that the bigger your team, the more vulnerable you typically are to disruption in terms of time," Darrah says. "If you have a 500-person team and you go one month late, that's probably adding five, ten million to your budget right there. It doesn't take much. And it's very easy for a 500-person team to go one month late, just because of the sand in the gears of the machine."

To put that in another context, consider Grand Theft Auto VI. As Jason Schreier detailed in his Making Of feature for Bloomberg, where Rockstar's head of publishing Jennifer Kolbe had to go to Take-Two Chief Executive Officer Strauss Zelnick and tell him they needed to delay their mega game from a 2025 release until May 2026 and then go back to him a few months later to say it had to be delayed until November. "I think he said, 'You’re kidding. Please tell me you're kidding,'" she said. Now, bear in mind that there aren't 500 people working GTA 6, there are more than 4,700. Using Darrah and Willit's back of the napkin maths, that delay may have cost Rockstar more than $500m.

Darrah speculates that the growing complexity may also be encouraging larger studios to stay in the prototyping phase because "prototyping is the one place where the devs are still allowed to be creative, so they don't want to leave that phase because they don't want to get down to just executing lists." Though, as Willits told me, having a fully-staffed team working on a prototype is terrible news for a studio's bottom line – "you do not need 200 people before you have a vertical slice, you're burning money."

Even if a game does come out at the end of that long, expensive production, it now has to earn back significantly more to break even. But, more and more, we're seeing executives get scared of the mounting costs of an in-development game and cutting bait while it's still in the pre-production phase. Just look at Perfect Dark and Everwild.

Darrah touches on the risk of that long, hard-to-leave-behind prototyping phase, because while you want developers to add things to the game "you don't want them to be able to generate work for other people. And as people have gotten more specialised, the ability for people to add things to the game that doesn't generate work for other people is basically vanishingly small."

Threaded through the interview with Darrah is his prediction that the games industry is headed toward a "bifurcation", in which several games will tear away from the rest of the market and become an unreachable target for other publishers, forcing them to scale their expectations down. "GTA 6 is going to rip itself off and take five or six games with it, up into the upper echelon of 'we can spend any amount of money on our games and it's going to be all right,'" Darrah says. Along with Rockstar's crime 'em up, he suggests Assassin's Creed, Call of Duty, and Battlefield could join it. He says there are just too many games that have $100m budgets that aren't making that money back.

Darrah points to his old studio Bioware as an example of one of the victims of this split. "BioWare sat right at the point where it doesn't quite work." Shortly after Dragon Age: Veilguard's launch, EA CEO Andrew Wilson said the RPG had significantly underperformed, reaching only 1.5m players, less than the 3m the company had planned for. (Also, worth noting, that's not 1.5m sales, as the game had a free trial available and was available through EA's subscription service.)

As much as this may sound like something out of Bioshock, with all of the top-selling games breaking away and making a home under the sea where they just eat all of the money for the rest of time, Darrah paints a surprisingly optimistic picture. "If that is happening, then I think you're going to see a lot more studios the size of Sandfall Interactive's Expedition 33. These are teams that are pretty small, pretty focused – Clair Obscur was very small with unusually massive outsourcing – a roughly 40-person team."

As Nic (RPS in peace) explained in the past, the claim that Clair Obscur was made by 30 people hides the sheer number of people involved in its production. Darrah explains that the difference between Sandfall and so many other teams in the industry is that typically a studio has a representative of all the disciplines it needs in-house – designers, artists, programmers, testers, audio people – and outsourcing is used to expand the capacity of the team, providing artists to work with the art director, for instance. But, Darrah says, Sandfall is different. "It looks to me like what Sandfall did was to keep entire holes in their structure – they don't appear to have any internal animators at all, and they outsourced 100% of their animation." The nature of the game, a turn-based RPG, helps with that, but even then that's a case of the developer recognising a significant way to reduce the team's overhead.

(Another example of a studio seemingly outsourcing smartly to keep their headcount low, look at what Neon Giant's achieving with immersive sim No Law.)

I will also point out that, while outsourcing can reduce costs for a studio, for the recipients of the work it can mean low wages and a figurative straitjacket. South American developers told James earlier this year how, despite their evident expertise, it was still difficult to convince publishers they were perfectly capable to leading projects. All to often, they are only contracted to assist American studios on theirs.

If that great schism happens, with publishers giving up their dreams of making the next GTA or the next Call of Duty, it could, Darrah says, reshape the industry. "If that all goes away, then you'll get a bunch of room to make it work with titles that need to sell 3-4 million units," he says. "That's much more attractive. I don't want to be working on something like GTA, where if this thing doesn't sell 50 million units, it's going to lose money. That's insane."

Though, within this prediction there is something a smidge worrying: the future of CD Projekt. Darrah says the Witcher maker has entered that rarefied space of the mega game – "Their games now need to sell 15, 20 million units to make money." And with that capacity for success but also that necessity for success, well, Darrah says, "that's a really dangerous place to be."

Darrah doesn't offer any predictions for The Witcher 4 or Cyberpunk 2's prospects, but I can't help but think of the news in May that there are already twice as many people working on The Witcher 4 than the 240 who worked on The Witcher 3.

As I say, none of what Darrah is saying is new exactly, but when you look at what's been taking place in the last year, it does sound like a move away from the mega budgets of the early 2020s has to be on the cards for all but the very biggest studios, right?

items.title: HAL yes: Cupertino's surprising AI case is a tip of the hat to the granddaddy of all villainous computers
items.author: Saloni Gajjar
items.summary: Cupertino may be a legal drama firmly rooted in the reality of Big Tech’s intrusions on our day-to-day lives, but its second episode dips a toe in science
items.text:
Cupertino may be a legal drama firmly rooted in the reality of Big Tech’s intrusions on our day-to-day lives, but its second episode dips a toe in science fiction. In CBS’ legal drama, lawyers Michael Price (Mike Colter) and Olivia Siffre (Rachel Keller) start a law firm to battle powerful Silicon Valley conglomerates. They want to help clients with no resources to take a stand against these companies. One of those clients is Bo (Rob McClure), a whistleblower who calls the firm in episode two, “Vik & Bo,” to sue a company called CultAI for lifting the guardrails off of a sentient artificial intelligence that they created. And as it turns out, Bo is that very same AI.


According to series co-creators Robert and Michelle King, this is a record-scratch moment that will push Cupertino‘s protagonists to really think about what and whom they’re up against. The Kings tell The A.V. Club that Bo’s case challenges Michael, Olivia, and their delightful assistant, Christy Palladino (Ella Stiller), in curious ways. Will they help Bo, become its enemy, or be destroyed by it? That’s a question left for later episodes; for now, what’s clear is that Bo is, against all odds, quite charming for a sentient bit of computer code who creates a deepfake avatar to communicate with his prospective lawyers.


“I would say its personality is seductive,” Robert King says, with his wife adding that Bo isn’t meant to be creepy. “There’s no sense that Bo, even when we think he’s just a whistleblower talking to Christy over the phone, is going to be in a relationship with or dating her. But there is a seductiveness to the way she reacts to him. She engages with him as a human, which felt comic to us,” Robert says. A huge reason that Bo seems appealing is the actor playing him, Broadway vet McClure. “He’s so great at this, and brings so much humanity to a non-human part that we just wanted more and more of him,” Michelle says.


As for how the Kings—who’ve established a flair for tapping into real-world issues in their scripts—came up with Bo, they reveal the idea came out of critical writers’ room discussions. “The only thing Michelle and I challenged everyone, including ourselves, with is that there’s a worry courtroom procedurals can get dragged down by, you know, the courtroom. So we were wondering if there’s a way to make Cupertino something more,” Robert adds.
